old.name: La Cafeotheque
old.label: 4th (near the Seine)
old.text: The earliest of them all, opened 2005 by Gloria Montenegro; the training ground where several later roasters cut their teeth (Sprudge; Paris by Mouth). Open in Google Maps →

old_also.name: La Caféothèque
old_also.label: Hôtel de Ville / riverside
old_also.hook: A rambling coffee 'temple' a block off the Seine, opened in 2005 by a former Guatemalan ambassador, with its own roastery and a long rotation of single-origin coffees - no blends - and worn armchairs made for sinking in with a cup and a book.
old_also.text: A rambling coffee 'temple' a block off the Seine, opened in 2005 by a former Guatemalan ambassador, with its own roastery and a long rotation of single-origin coffees - no blends - and worn armchairs made for sinking in with a cup and a book. Signal One of the roasters that taught Paris to take coffee seriously; calm and unhurried, though it closes by early evening. Come for the coffee first and the laptop second.

old.name: Belleville Brulerie
old.label: 19th (Belleville)
old.text: The micro-roastery, founded 2013 by Thomas Lehoux, David Flynn and Anselme Blayney, that lit the fuse of Paris specialty coffee and now supplies much of the city (Gault&Millau; Sprudge). Open in Google Maps →

old.name: Telescope
old.label: 1st (rue Villedo)
old.text: Opened 2012 by Nicolas Clerc, a tiny Right-Bank pioneer of the scene, listed by Le Fooding and Paris by Mouth. Open in Google Maps →

old.name: Salle Ovale, BnF Richelieu
old.label: Bourse / Richelieu
old.hook: The most beautiful free reading room in Paris: a vast oval hall under a glazed dome, holding some 20,000 open-access books (9,000 of them comics) and 160 seats where anyone at all can sit and work the whole day.
old.text: The most beautiful free reading room in Paris: a vast oval hall under a glazed dome, holding some 20,000 open-access books (9,000 of them comics) and 160 seats where anyone at all can sit and work the whole day. Signal Free, no library card, no appointment for the Oval Room - just walk in, sign the Wi-Fi policy, and stay until closing. Closed Mondays. The one grand room in the city that asks nothing of you.

old.name: Bibliothèque Mazarine
old.label: Institut de France
old.hook: The oldest public library in France, Cardinal Mazarin's own collection opened to scholars in 1643, its bust-lined seventeenth-century hall on the Seine still a working reading room, not a museum piece.
old.text: The oldest public library in France, Cardinal Mazarin's own collection opened to scholars in 1643, its bust-lined seventeenth-century hall on the Seine still a working reading room, not a museum piece. Signal Free, but you show ID and are issued a reader's pass on the spot before you can settle in to work; closed annually 1-15 August. Expect a scholar's silence, not a café hum.

old.name: Anticafé
old.label: Louvre / Beaubourg and five more
old.hook: The pay-for-time coworking café: about 5 euros an hour - the tab auto-caps around 24 euros for a full day - buys unlimited coffee, snacks, fast Wi-Fi and a seat you are meant to keep, with a small library and board games for the breaks.
old.text: The pay-for-time coworking café: about 5 euros an hour - the tab auto-caps around 24 euros for a full day - buys unlimited coffee, snacks, fast Wi-Fi and a seat you are meant to keep, with a small library and board games for the breaks. Signal The guilt-free answer to Parisian laptop-wariness - you are paying for the time, not the coffee. Seven branches across the city; reserve ahead for groups of four or more.

old.name: Café de Flore
old.label: Saint-Germain-des-Prés
old.hook: The 1887 café where Sartre and Beauvoir sat out the war in the warmth and James Baldwin wrote much of Go Tell It on the Mountain upstairs over cognac and coffee. Red banquettes, marble, mirrors - unchanged, on purpose.
old.text: The 1887 café where Sartre and Beauvoir sat out the war in the warmth and James Baldwin wrote much of Go Tell It on the Mountain upstairs over cognac and coffee. Red banquettes, marble, mirrors - unchanged, on purpose. Signal Touristy and dear; a small coffee costs what a full lunch does elsewhere. But the quieter first floor is where you actually linger, and once, for the ghosts, it earns the price.

old.name: Les Deux Magots
old.label: Place Saint-Germain-des-Prés
old.hook: Trading as a café since 1884, named for the two carved Chinese figures - the magots - perched on a pillar inside, gazing down over the room; Hemingway, Beauvoir and the Surrealists were regulars. Live jazz on Thursday evenings.
old.text: Trading as a café since 1884, named for the two carved Chinese figures - the magots - perched on a pillar inside, gazing down over the room; Hemingway, Beauvoir and the Surrealists were regulars. Live jazz on Thursday evenings. Signal Flore's next-door rival and just as expensive; take a terrace table facing Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the oldest church in Paris, and nurse a single drink - no waiter will ever hurry you off it.

old.name: Le Select
old.label: Montparnasse
old.hook: The 1923 café Hemingway called 'the soul of Montparnasse,' once open around the clock, still running past midnight with black-and-white waiters and marble tables you can hold for hours.
old.text: The 1923 café Hemingway called 'the soul of Montparnasse,' once open around the clock, still running past midnight with black-and-white waiters and marble tables you can hold for hours. Signal The least gentrified of the Montparnasse legends - a genuine neighbourhood brasserie rather than a museum. Come late, when it keeps going long after the tourist cafés have shuttered.

old.name: Le Pavillon des Canaux
old.label: Bassin de la Villette
old.hook: A former canal-inspector's house on the water, opened in 2014 as half-café, half-coworking room: work in a former bedroom, or literally in a bathtub, over locally roasted coffee with the Bassin de la Villette out the window.
old.text: A former canal-inspector's house on the water, opened in 2014 as half-café, half-coworking room: work in a former bedroom, or literally in a bathtub, over locally roasted coffee with the Bassin de la Villette out the window. Signal Genuinely built for working - laptops welcome by day, Wi-Fi that holds, open to midnight (1am Thursday to Saturday) - though not every room allows them. The most unpretentious work spot on this list.

old.name: Ten Belles
old.label: Canal Saint-Martin
old.hook: A pocket-sized specialty roaster and sourdough bakery just off the canal, pouring some of the best flat whites in the city since 2012 from a counter locals actually queue at.
old.text: A pocket-sized specialty roaster and sourdough bakery just off the canal, pouring some of the best flat whites in the city since 2012 from a counter locals actually queue at. Signal Too small to camp in - take a sharp coffee and a slice of bread, then a bench by the water. Superb coffee, wrong room for a long session; be honest with yourself about which you need.

old_also.name: Ten Belles
old_also.label: 10th (Canal Saint-Martin)
old_also.text: One of the original specialty cafes, pouring Belleville Brulerie beans — a template the city copied (European Coffee Trip; Paris by Mouth). Open in Google Maps →

old.name: Café Craft
old.label: Canal Saint-Martin
old.hook: A café designed from the studs up for people who came to work: long communal tables, an outlet at every seat, steady Wi-Fi and a calm room of designers, coders and writers near the canal.
old.text: A café designed from the studs up for people who came to work: long communal tables, an outlet at every seat, steady Wi-Fi and a calm room of designers, coders and writers near the canal. Signal Here the laptop is the norm, not something merely tolerated - the honest choice when a grand café would quietly resent you. You pay café prices for a desk you can keep all afternoon.

old.name: Giverny
old.label: ~1h15 NW (train to Vernon + shuttle), on the Normandy border
old.hook: Monet's house and the Japanese water garden with the lily pond and the green bridge.
old.text: Monet's house and the Japanese water garden with the lily pond and the green bridge. The paintings were made here and the garden is the original, replanted each year to Monet's own palette. Season only: open roughly April to 1 November and closed all winter, so plan around it.

old.name: Auvers-sur-Oise
old.label: ~1h N by train (Val-d'Oise)
old.hook: Van Gogh's last chapter: the tiny Auberge Ravoux room where he died, the church he painted, the wheatfields, and his grave beside his brother Theo.
old.text: Van Gogh's last chapter: the tiny Auberge Ravoux room where he died, the church he painted, the wheatfields, and his grave beside his brother Theo. The most concentrated stretch of a painter's final days you can walk in a single afternoon: roughly 70 canvases made in his last 70 days, and the honest, un-touristed melancholy that goes with it.

old.name: Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pignons
old.label: ~1h S
old.hook: Twenty-five thousand hectares of oak, white sand and sandstone boulders, with the royal chateau of Fontainebleau at its edge.
old.text: Twenty-five thousand hectares of oak, white sand and sandstone boulders, with the royal chateau of Fontainebleau at its edge. The oldest and biggest bouldering ground on earth: the 'Font' grade was born here, there are thousands of numbered problems on soft sandy landings, and it is the same rock and dappled light that pulled the Barbizon painters out of Paris.

old_also.name: Barbizon
old_also.label: ~1h S, on the edge of the Fontainebleau forest
old_also.hook: One cobbled street of former painters' studios, the Auberge Ganne where they gathered, and the preserved houses of Millet and Rousseau.
old_also.text: One cobbled street of former painters' studios, the Auberge Ganne where they gathered, and the preserved houses of Millet and Rousseau. Plein-air landscape painting was effectively invented here in the 1830s, a generation before Impressionism: Millet, Rousseau and Corot fled the city to paint peasants and trees on this exact forest edge.

around:Fontainebleau & Barbizon.brief: Merge the old 'Foret de Fontainebleau & Trois Pignons' card and the old 'Barbizon' card into one day out (the forest's bouldering and the painters' village). Day-trip labels.

around:Versailles.brief: NEW day-trip card: the Château de Versailles — the trip (RER C to Versailles Château Rive Gauche, or train from Saint-Lazare/Montparnasse), closed Mondays, timed tickets, 2026 passport price (verify on chateauversailles.fr), the gardens, Trianon, the Potager du Roi (the king's kitchen garden, still worked by the École nationale supérieure de paysage — a cook's angle). Labels Getting there · Time needed · Don't miss · Eat (no restaurant names unless verified). maps_query 'Château de Versailles'.

old.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte
old.label: ~55 min SE (near Melun)
old.hook: The first great collaboration of Le Vau, Le Brun and the gardener Le Notre; candlelit evenings with fountains in summer.
old.text: The first great collaboration of Le Vau, Le Brun and the gardener Le Notre; candlelit evenings with fountains in summer. The dress rehearsal for Versailles, and honestly the more moving visit: it was so beautiful it got its owner Fouquet arrested by a jealous Louis XIV, who then poached the entire creative team. Far less mobbed than Versailles itself.

old.name: Chantilly
old.label: ~40 min N by train (Oise, just over the regional line)
old.hook: A chateau floating on its own reflecting pond, the Musee Conde old-master collection, and the vast Grandes Ecuries horse museum.
old.text: A chateau floating on its own reflecting pond, the Musee Conde old-master collection, and the vast Grandes Ecuries horse museum. The Conde paintings hang exactly as the last duke willed them: no loans, no rehang, a frozen 19th-century picture gallery often called the richest in France after the Louvre. And yes, the town lays claim to creme Chantilly.

around:Provins.group: A walled town and a river dance

old.name: Provins
old.label: ~1h25 SE by train (Seine-et-Marne), UNESCO listed
old.hook: An intact medieval walled town: over a mile of 12th-century ramparts, the Tour Cesar keep, underground galleries and rose gardens.
old.text: An intact medieval walled town: over a mile of 12th-century ramparts, the Tour Cesar keep, underground galleries and rose gardens. A survivor of the medieval Champagne trade fairs, preserved in stone rather than restored to look old; the rosa gallica rose trade is woven into the town's identity and its shops.

around:Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pec.group: A walled town and a river dance

old.name: Guinguette de l'Ile du Martin-Pecheur
old.label: ~40 min E by RER, Champigny-sur-Marne (94)
old.hook: Across the water to a small island in the Marne (it trades today as 'La Nouvelle Guinguette'): accordion musette, fried fish and white wine under the arbours, salsa on Sunday evenings.
old.text: Across the water to a small island in the Marne (it trades today as 'La Nouvelle Guinguette'): accordion musette, fried fish and white wine under the arbours, salsa on Sunday evenings. The living remnant of the riverside guinguettes the Impressionists painted (Renoir's boating-party world). Revived in 1993, it keeps the tradition going literally out on the water, well off the tourist map.
